# ECON 0100 | Demo C

## Patronus Lessons

Every winter, dementors drift through Hogsmeade, and the surest defense against them is the Patronus Charm. Private tutors sell lessons in the charm. Each witch or wizard who learns it also protects their neighbors from dementors, an external benefit of 10 Coins per lesson. Prices are in coins and quantity is in lessons. The Demand (Marginal Private Benefit) and Supply (Marginal Cost) equations for lessons are the following:

$$
D: P_b = 40 - Q_d \qquad\qquad S: P_s = 10 + Q_s
$$

### C1.2 | Patronus Lessons

The graph shows the market for lessons: marginal private benefit (MPB), marginal social benefit (MSB), and supply (S)The lettered regions are for the questions.

::: {.table style=plain inset=4pt columns="auto 1fr" spans=r0c0:2x1 aligns=r0c0:default}

|   |   |
| :--- | :--- |
| MSB lies \_\_\_\_\_ coins above MPB at every quantity |   |
| Market Quantity ($\hat{Q}$): | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Efficient Quantity ($Q^*$): | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Deadweight Loss (*letter*): | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Deadweight Loss (*area*): | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| MSB of the Last Lesson Traded: | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| MC of the Last Lesson Traded: | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| The Market Trades: | $\square$ too many $\quad\square$ too few lessons |

:::

 

 

 

::::: solution

MSB lies $10$ coins above MPB. Market Quantity $\hat{Q}$: $15$ lessons. Efficient Quantity $Q^*$: $20$ lessons. Deadweight Loss Region: B. Deadweight Loss: $25$ coins. Last lesson traded: $MSB = 35$, $MC = 25$. The market trades too few lessons.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: column

Each lesson is worth its buyer MPB and another $10$ to the neighbors it protects, so MSB is MPB shifted up by $10$ at every quantity:

$$
MSB = MPB + 10 = 50 - Q
$$

Buyers count only their own benefit, so the market trades where MPB meets supply:

$$
40 - Q = 10 + Q \quad\Rightarrow\quad \hat{Q} = 15, \quad \hat{P} = 25
$$

Efficiency counts the neighbors too, so it needs MSB to meet supply:

$$
50 - Q = 10 + Q \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q^* = 20, \quad P = 30
$$

:::

::: column

![Patronus lessons with region B, the deadweight loss, in red](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::::

The deadweight loss is B, the triangle between MSB and supply over lessons $15$ to $20$. Each of those lessons is worth more to society than it costs, yet none is traded: at $Q = 15$ the last lesson has $MSB = 35$ and $MC = 25$ (read off the price axis), so one more lesson would add $10$ more in benefit than it costs, and the market trades too few. The height at $Q = 15$ is the external benefit of $10$ and the base is the $5$ lessons the market skips:

$$
\text{DWL} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times (20 - 15) = 25
$$

A is the external benefit the $15$ traded lessons already deliver. C, between supply and MPB, is how far each of lessons $16$ to $20$ costs more than its buyer alone would pay, which is why the market skips them; it is not a loss to society.

:::::

\newpage

### C2.2 | A Subsidy for Lessons

To encourage lessons, the Ministry pays tutors a subsidy of 8 coins per lesson. For this question, ignore the external benefit: demand is the marginal benefit (MB) of a lesson.

::: {.table style=plain inset=4pt columns="auto 1fr"}

|   |   |
| :--- | :--- |
| Buyer’s Price ($P_b$): | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Seller’s Price ($P_s$): | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Subsidy Quantity ($Q^{Sub}$): | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Deadweight Loss (*DWL*): | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Last Lesson Traded, MC vs. MB: | $\square$ above $\quad\square$ below |

:::

::::: solution

Buyer’s Price $P_b$: $21$ coins. Seller’s Price $P_s$: $29$ coins. Subsidy Quantity $Q^{Sub}$: $19$ lessons. Deadweight Loss: $16$ coins. For the last lesson traded, MC is above MB.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: column

Ignoring the external benefit, demand is the marginal benefit, and the market without the subsidy is efficient: $40 - Q = 10 + Q$ gives $Q = 15$ at $P = 25$.

A subsidy is the tax wedge turned around: the seller now receives $8$ more than the buyer pays, so the wedge sits to the *right* of $15$:

$$
P_s = P_b + 8 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 10 + Q = (40 - Q) + 8 \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 19
$$

so $P_b = 40 - 19 = 21$ and $P_s = 10 + 19 = 29$.

:::

::: column

![An 8-coin subsidy on Patronus lessons, ignoring the external benefit](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::::

At $Q = 19$, the last lesson costs $MC = 29$ to provide but is worth only $MB = 21$ to its buyer, so MC is above MB. The same is true of every lesson from $16$ to $19$: each trades only because the Ministry pays the difference. The triangle between supply and demand over those $4$ lessons is the deadweight loss:

$$
\text{DWL} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 8 \times (19 - 15) = 16
$$

Counting the external benefit of $10$ is a corrective-policy question (C3.1): the efficient quantity becomes $20$, and a subsidy of exactly $10$ would reach it.

:::::

\newpage

## Flummoxed by the Floo Powder Fiasco

Floo Powder is a magical commodity used by witches and wizards to transport themselves through fireplaces to different locations. While it’s often convenient, its use is associated with negative environmental effects, including air pollution and the depletion of magical resources used to produce the powder. The Ministry’s Bureau of Economic Analysis has estimated the externality to be 12 coins per tin with the following supply and demand equations:

$$
D: P_b = 120 - 2 Q_d \qquad\qquad S: P_s = Q_s
$$

### C1.1 | The Fiasco

Start by using a graph and algebra to describe the market failure.

::: {.table style=plain inset=4pt columns="auto 1fr" spans=r0c0:2x1 aligns=r0c0:default}

|   |   |
| :--- | :--- |
| Graph demand, supply, and MSC, and shade the deadweight loss. |   |
| Marginal Social Cost (MSC): | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Market Quantity ($\hat{Q}$): | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Efficient Quantity ($Q^*$): | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Deadweight Loss (*DWL*): | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| The Market Trades: | $\square$ too much $\quad\square$ too little |

:::

 

::::: solution

Marginal Social Cost: $MSC = 12 + Q$. Market Quantity $\hat{Q}$: $40$ tins. Efficient Quantity $Q^*$: $36$ tins. Deadweight Loss: $24$ coins. The market trades too much.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: column

The sellers’ marginal cost is the supply curve, $P = Q$. Each tin also costs everyone else $12$, so marginal social cost is supply shifted up by $12$:

$$
MSC = 12 + Q
$$

The market ignores the external cost and trades where demand meets supply:

$$
120 - 2Q = Q \quad\Rightarrow\quad \hat{Q} = 40, \quad \hat{P} = 40
$$

Efficiency needs demand (marginal benefit) to meet MSC:

$$
120 - 2Q = 12 + Q \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q^* = 36, \quad P = 48
$$

:::

::: column

![Floo Powder market failure with the deadweight loss shaded](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::::

The deadweight loss is the triangle between MSC and demand over tins $36$ to $40$, with corners $(36, 48)$, $(40, 52)$ and $(40, 40)$. Its height at $Q = 40$ is the external cost of $12$ and its base is the $4$ extra tins, so $\text{DWL} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 12 \times (40 - 36) = 24$.

At $Q = 40$, $MSC = 12 + 40 = 52$ and $MB = 120 - 80 = 40$. The last tin costs society $12$ more than it is worth to its buyer, and the same is true of every tin from $36$ to $40$, so the market trades too much.

:::::

\newpage

### C2.1 | A Tax for Revenue

Needing revenue, and not yet knowing the size of the externality, the Ministry imposes a tax of 6 coins per tin on Floo Powder. For this question, ignore the external cost.

::: {.table style=plain inset=4pt columns="auto 1fr"}

|   |   |
| :--- | :--- |
| Buyer’s Price ($P_b$): | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Seller’s Price ($P_s$): | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Post-Tax Quantity ($Q^{Tax}$): | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Tax Incidence on Buyers: | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Tax Incidence on Sellers: | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Deadweight Loss (*DWL*): | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Who Bears More of the Tax? | $\square$ buyers $\quad\square$ sellers $\quad\square$ equal |

:::

 

::::: solution

Buyer’s Price $P_b$: $44$ coins. Seller’s Price $P_s$: $38$ coins. Post-Tax Quantity $Q^{Tax}$: $38$ tins. Tax Incidence: buyers $4$, sellers $2$. Deadweight Loss: $6$ coins. Who bears more: buyers.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: column

Before the tax, buyers and sellers face one price, $P = 40$ at $Q = 40$ (C1.1). With the tax, the buyer price sits $6$ above the seller price:

$$
P_b = P_s + 6 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 120 - 2Q = Q + 6 \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 38
$$

so $P_b = 120 - 76 = 44$ and $P_s = 38$. Check: $44 - 38 = 6$.

:::

::: column

![A 6-coin tax on Floo Powder](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::::

Incidence: buyers pay $44 - 40 = 4$ more than before and sellers receive $40 - 38 = 2$ less, and the two add to the $6$ tax. Buyers bear more because demand is steeper than supply (slope $2$ against $1$): buyers are the side less able to move away from the tax.

Ignoring the external cost, the untaxed market’s $40$ tins were efficient, so the tax destroys the surplus on the $2$ tins it prevents, the triangle between demand and supply from $38$ to $40$:

$$
\text{DWL} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times (40 - 38) = 6
$$

Counting the external cost of $12$ turns this around: those $2$ tins cost society more than they were worth, so the tax moves the market *toward* the efficient $36$. That is the C3.1 question.

:::::

\newpage

### C3.1 | Designing the Policy

The Ministry of Magic has hired you to design a policy that corrects the market failure caused by the negative externality of Floo Powder use. Propose the policy you recommend and how it would impact the market for Floo Powder and its users.

::: {.table style=plain inset=4pt columns="auto 1fr"}

|   |   |
| :--- | :--- |
| Policy Type: | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Policy Size: | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Post-Policy Quantity ($Q^{\tau}$): | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Post-Policy Deadweight Loss: | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Post-Policy Quantity vs. Efficient: | $\square$ above $\quad\square$ at $\quad\square$ below |

:::

::::: solution

Policy Type: a per-unit tax. Policy Size: $12$ coins per tin. Post-Policy Quantity $Q^{\tau}$: $36$ tins, at the efficient quantity. Post-Policy Deadweight Loss: $0$.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: column

The externality is a cost, so the policy is a tax, and its size is the external cost per tin, $12$. Sellers then pay the full social cost: supply plus the tax is $12 + Q$, exactly MSC. The buyer price sits $12$ above the seller price:

$$
P_b = P_s + 12 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 120 - 2Q = Q + 12 \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 36
$$

so $P_b = 120 - 72 = 48$ and $P_s = 36$.

:::

::: column

![A 12-coin corrective tax on Floo Powder](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::::

Without a policy the market trades $40$ tins. The tax moves it down to $36$, exactly the efficient quantity, so the deadweight loss from C1.1 is gone. Users of Floo Powder pay $48$ instead of $40$ and buy $4$ fewer tins; sellers keep $36$ instead of $40$. (The Ministry collects $12 \times 36 = 432$ coins; not required.)

The $6$-coin tax in C2.1 moved quantity from $40$ to $38$, the right direction but not far enough: $38$ is still above the efficient $36$, because the tax is smaller than the external cost, and it leaves a deadweight loss of $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times (38 - 36) = 6$, the gap between MSC ($50$) and demand ($44$) at $38$. The tins from $36$ to $38$ still cost society more than they are worth.

:::::
